questions.explain: SQL Server drivers (ADO.NET SqlClient, ODBC, JDBC) pool in the client: the pool lives in each application process, keyed on the exact connection string (one differing character = separate pool). Pooling is on by default; there is no proxy to deploy (RDS Proxy doesn't support SQL Server), but also nothing to tune centrally — which is why waste hides in application defaults for years.

questions.explain: ADO.NET defaults to Max Pool Size=100 per process per connection string: 20 web servers × 4 worker processes × 2 connection strings = up to 16,000 pooled connections against a database that sees only dozens of concurrent requests. Size from measured concurrency: set Max Pool to peak concurrent requests + headroom (e.g., peak 12 → 25), Min Pool Size=0 unless warm-start latency is measured.

questions.explain: The expensive anti-patterns: Pooling=False, connection strings that differ per service/environment (string sprawl = separate pools), and building the connection string per call with embedded timestamps/GUIDs — every distinct string creates a brand-new pool, so the app effectively runs unpooled while believing it's pooled. Also check unclosed readers without CommandBehavior.CloseConnection and long-lived EF DbContexts.

questions.explain: Each pooled connection consumes worker threads, session state, and network buffers — 1,000 idle connections can pin hundreds of MB and exhaust max worker threads on smaller classes, forcing a larger instance. Dropping steady-state sessions from 1,200 to 150 can allow a db.r5.2xlarge → db.r5.xlarge right-size (~40–50% compute saving, plus the License-Included bill shrinks); on Azure SQL, high max_session_percent with low CPU means the tier is consumed by connections, not queries — fix pooling before scaling.

questions.explain: Leaks show as steadily climbing session counts that never fall after load subsides, ending in 'Timeout expired...obtaining a connection from the pool'; the fix is in code: using blocks (dispose returns the connection even on exception). Server-side, alert on sessions sleeping >1 hour from app logins, run a weekly automated audit flagging instances where idle-over-30-min ratio > 70% with > 50 sessions, and remediate in order: standardize strings, bound pool sizes, fix leaks, then resize.
